title: A Primer for Naming Day, for Children Who Can Nearly Read
author: written out by Hesta Hollins for the children of Merrowby, with pictures by the children
body:
# A Primer for Naming Day

*For children who can nearly read. Ask a grown person for the long words. There are four.*

## What happens

In the spring, on Naming Day, every child born since the last one is stood on the mounting-block by the well and told their name.

Not asked. **Told.** Loudly. By somebody who is not their mother, so that it comes from the village and not from the house.

Then everybody says it back. Everybody. All of them, at once, and then three times more, and the third time is always the loudest because by then people have found their voice and are enjoying themselves.

Then there is cake, and somebody's uncle falls in the horse trough. That part is not in the custom but it has happened eleven years running.

## Why we say it back

Because a name said by one person is a word, and a name said by eighty people is a **rope**.

You know how you can shout in the dry valley and hear yourself come back? A name is like that, except the valley is everybody you know, and it does not stop coming back for as long as they keep saying it.

Things that nobody says go quiet. That is not a story to frighten you with. If it were a story to frighten you with, it would have a monster in it, and it does not have anything in it at all, which is the trouble.

## The four long words

**Tending.** Everything you do with care and with other people. Cooking counts. Mending counts. Being told off for scratching snail-tables on the well counts, because it means somebody is looking at you.

**Renown.** How many people say your name when you are not there. You do not get this by asking. You get it by doing something in front of people who talk, and in Merrowby that is everybody.

**Hollow.** What people go when they stop being kind. You would know it if you saw it. Everybody says you would not, and everybody is wrong; the dogs know first.

**Hearth.** The other way. Warm hands, and people glad to see you, and the fire at your house being the sort of fire other people come and sit at.

## Things to do on Naming Day

1. Say the new baby's name three times, properly, not in a silly voice.
2. Say the names of the three quiet villages after Old Pellam says them at the bell. You will not know what they mean. Say them anyway. They are: Larkstead, Gosford, and one more, and if Pellam only says two this year do not ask him why in front of people.
3. Learn your own family's bell. It is in the lane. Yours is the one that sounds like *your* one; you will know it and you will not be able to explain it, and that is correct.
4. Carry something to somebody's door. A loaf is best. One loaf is a sentence, two is a conversation, three is a friendship. Nobody knows who decided this. It has never once failed.

## The last thing

If you are ever somewhere with a name on it — a village, a well, a hill, a dog — say the name out loud once before you leave.

It costs nothing.

It might be nothing.

It might not.

title: The Long Table Book: Hearthvale Cookery
author: Maud Brambling, baker of Merrowby, who has been asked eleven times and has finally done it
body:
# The Long Table Book

*Eleven people have asked me to write this down and I have said no eleven times, because a receipt written down is a receipt that stops being asked for, and the asking is half of it. Here it is anyway. Read it at my oven and I will tell you the rest.*

## Chalk-crust hearth loaf

Barley and wheat, two to one. Your own barm, not bought; bought barm is somebody else's kitchen and it tastes of their kitchen. Salt, a good pinch and then the same again, because you will be timid the first time and everybody is.

Prove it warm and **prove it twice**. A single prove makes a loaf; a double prove makes a loaf people come back for, and that is the whole trade.

Bake it on the stone, not in a tin. The crust goes chalk-white and it will look burnt underneath and it is not.

*The first loaf of the day is not for sale.* It goes on the rim-stone at the crater and you walk away and you do not look back to see who takes it. My mother did it and her mother did it. If you ask me why I will give you a short answer about folk on the road. Ask me twice and I will tell you that there are people who used to come to this market who do not any more, and that nobody can remember which, and that a warm loaf left where they would have walked is the least a person can do about that.

## Seedcake for Tollday

Caraway and honey, and the honey wants to be hedge-honey, dark, off the downs. There was a woman who sold it on the end stall. I bought from her for twenty years. I will not write her name here because I have written it wrong twice already and it will not come right.

## Wassail, which is new, and which I did not approve of

Mullard's dark ale and Bessa Tamwick's cider, equal, warmed, with an apple roasted in it and a nutmeg if a boat has been in.

Twenty years those two have fought over the head of the Long Table and a stranger put them in one bowl and now we all have to live with it. It is good. I said that in the Lip and Corwen went out of the room.

## Nine-day pottage

Root vegetables, a ham bone, and whatever else. Keep it on the back of the fire for nine days, adding as you go, never emptying. Every Vale kitchen has one. It is not a receipt, it is a habit, and a house with a cold pot has something wrong in it and the village will know within a week.

## On flour, since I am asked

Buy from Pennywort. Twopence the measure and the measure is honest and the steward weighs it twice a month out of spite, which is the best guarantee in Hearthvale.

And if a sack ever comes to you that keeps a month when it should keep a fortnight, and never moulds, and makes a bread that tastes of nothing at all — not bad, *nothing* — do not bake it and do not throw it in the stream. Take it to the hedge-witch. She will want it, she will pay for it, and she will not tell you why for about a year.

## The only rule

Cook for somebody. Food made for one person eaten alone is fuel. I have fed this village for forty years and I have never once got the salt right cooking for myself.

title: A True and Compleat Account of the Beasts of the Basin
author: Hob Larkin, hunter, of no fixed lodge
body:
# A True and Compleat Account of the Beasts of the Basin

*Being the fruit of thirty-one years afield by the finest hunter of his generation, who is me.*

## The down wolf

Grey-gold, lean, and **cowardly**, which is why they circle. They will not face a man who faces them. I have stood down a pack of nine with a billhook and a hard look.

*(Later hand, in pencil, throughout: 'Three. It was three, I was there, and he was up a thorn tree. — T. Cresswell')*

They lunge when you turn away, so the trick is never to turn away, which I have taught to hundreds.

## The bristleback

A boar in armour of its own hair. Charges straight and cannot turn, so step aside at the last moment and take it behind the shoulder.

This is true and is the only honest sentence in the book. *(pencil: 'Agreed. — T.C.')*

## The hedge-wight

A farmer buried with his tools who did not stop working.

Do not read what follows to children. They come up out of the barrows on the nights of no moon in numbers of forty and fifty and go through the hedges *scything in step*, and I have seen this from a hilltop, and the hair of my head has never lain flat since.

*(pencil: 'He saw two. They were not in step. One was in a ditch. — T.C.')*

What is certain is that they are slow, they will not be turned aside by shouting, and their poise is enormous; you may hit one four times and it does not notice, and the fifth time it notices and you are in the hedge.

**They will not pass the Singing Yew.** That is not a story. The old yew on the Tamwick side with the bell grown into its heart hums in any wind, and a wight walking at it will stop, and stand, and turn and go another way. The orchard men rely on it. Nobody knows why and the one Sayer I told laughed at me and then wrote it down when he thought I was not looking.

## The sallowjaw of the marsh

Lies in the water as a log. I have taken eleven.

*(pencil: 'Two.')*

The method is to walk the bank and watch for a log that is against the current. A log that is against the current is a lie.

## The wisp

A lantern that is not a lantern. It goes before you in the fog and it is *helpful*, which is how it gets you, because a light in a marsh at night is the most persuasive thing in the world.

Walk to a wisp and you will walk into deep water. I know a man this happened to and he was a better hunter than me, and I have not been in the marsh at night since, and I will not be talked into it.

*(pencil: 'This entry is true, is not boastful, and is the only one he will not discuss in the Lip. The man was his brother. — T.C.')*

## The crag-wolf, the scree-hag, the stone-thrall

Of the north I say only this: everything there is larger, whiter and less interested in you than you expect, and the ones that are interested are the ones you do not see.

I have not been north. I am not going north. A hunter who claims the whole basin is a liar, and I would rather be found out on the wolves than on the mountains.

title: The Falling of the Toll: a play for the Long Table
author: Merrick Gosling, after an older version by his master, after an older version than that
body:
# The Falling of the Toll

*A play for the Long Table. Four parts and a Crowd. The Crowd is everyone at the table and needs no rehearsal, which is the point of it.*

**PERSONS:** The Bell-Maker. The Daughter. The Warden (there were no Wardens yet; nobody has ever cared). The Crowd.

---

**BELL-MAKER.** I have made a bell so great that when it sounds, the valley will hold.

**CROWD.** *(banging the table)* Hold! Hold! Hold!

**DAUGHTER.** Father, the tower is thin.

**BELL-MAKER.** The tower is as thin as it needs to be. Everything is as thin as it needs to be, until it isn't.

*(This line is spoken as a joke and lands as one, every year, and every year there is a pause after it that nobody plans.)*

**DAUGHTER.** Then ring it and be done.

**BELL-MAKER.** Not yet. A bell struck once is struck for ever; it goes on sounding whether you hear it or not. I will not strike it until I know what note the valley wants.

**WARDEN.** And how long have you been finding out?

**BELL-MAKER.** Forty years.

**CROWD.** *(groaning)* Forty years!

---

**DAUGHTER.** *(alone)* He will never strike it. He is afraid of the note. So I will climb up, and I will strike it once, and then it will be done and he can come down to supper.

*(She climbs. In Merrowby she climbs on a table. In Tamwick they use a ladder, which is showing off.)*

**DAUGHTER.** *(striking)* There!

*(THE CROWD makes the sound. Everyone. One note, held as long as the breath lasts, and the last voice to stop is cheered. This is the whole reason the play exists.)*

---

**WARDEN.** The tower is coming down.

**BELL-MAKER.** Let it. The bell is struck.

**DAUGHTER.** Father, I am sorry —

**BELL-MAKER.** Don't be sorry. Be quick. *(He puts her off the tower. He does not come down.)*

*(The bell falls. The Crowd bangs the table once, hard, and stops dead. The silence after is the longest silence in the Vale calendar and no child has ever got through it without laughing, and the laughing is allowed.)*

---

**WARDEN.** *(in the crater)* It is cracked.

**DAUGHTER.** It is still sounding.

**WARDEN.** I hear nothing.

**DAUGHTER.** No. But the grass is green where it fell, and it was not green before, and there was no valley here that a person could farm, and now there is, and my father is under it.

**WARDEN.** Then what do we do?

**DAUGHTER.** We live on it. And once a year we all make the noise, so that it is not only the bell that is sounding.

**CROWD.** *(the note again, everyone, badly)*

---

*Note from the copyist.* The last exchange is new. My master had the Daughter die in the fall and the Warden speak alone, and it played better and I have taken it out anyway.

Last spring the Toll began to hum, and this play stopped being a story about a thing that happened and became a story about a thing that is happening, and I will not have it end with everybody dead and one man talking.

If it hums at the Long Table while we are doing it, keep going. Do not stop and look at the hill. The note is the same note; we have been making it badly once a year for a thousand years, and I have come to think that is not a coincidence.

title: Charts and Cautions for the Salt Isles
author: Nauve Mor, trader, who has been three times and intends a fourth
body:
# Charts and Cautions for the Salt Isles

*For anyone fool enough to go west past the tide-flats. I have been three times. I intend a fourth, which tells you what my judgement is worth.*

## Getting there

Out of Isseva on the ebb, down the channels, and keep the lantern poles on your right until they stop, and they do stop, and the stopping is the worst hour of the voyage because there is nothing to count.

Then tide-flats: eleven miles of wet sand at low water, sea at high, and nothing in between that will hold a boat or a foot. You cross on the flood in a flat boat and you do not stop, and if the fog comes down you anchor and sit and you do not follow any light you see, whatever it is doing, however much it looks like a man with a lamp waving you in.

Then the Grey Sea, which is grey.

## The Isles

Seven that are inhabited. The salt-traders speak Sedgish with a lisp and think our Sedgish is the lisp, and they are very funny about it and it takes about three days to stop being annoyed.

They live off salt pans, sea-birds and charts. **They sell charts of drowned cities.** This is the whole reason anyone goes.

## On the charts

Here is what I will say, having bought four.

They are beautiful. They are drawn on skin and coloured with something that does not run. They show street plans, harbour moles, and the names of wards, in a script that nobody on the Isles can read and that they will tell you cheerfully they cannot read.

Two of my four match each other in every particular, and they were bought eleven years apart from unrelated families on different islands.

One of them shows a ring of twelve towers around a central hall.

I took that one to a Sayer in Tollmere. She looked at it for some time and asked me what I wanted for it, and when I said it was not for sale she asked again, in a different voice, and I left.

## Cautions

**Do not ask where the cities were.** They will tell you west, and point, and there is nothing west; I have sailed two days west of the furthest isle and there is nothing but the same grey.

**Do not haggle over food.** Salt is their coin and food is not; offering marks for a meal is an insult and offering to help carry salt is not.

**Do not be a loud guest.** They are quiet in the way the marsh is quiet, and for the same reason, whatever that reason is.

**Bring apples.** I took six Tamwick apples the second time and came home with a chart I could not have afforded in silver. They had heard of apples. None of them had seen one. A woman of eighty ate one, slowly, in front of her whole family, and then put the core in a box.

## Why I am going again

Because on the third voyage an old man asked me whether the bell in our basin was still sounding.

I said it had cracked and fallen a thousand years ago.

He said: *that is not what I asked you.*
